source_spans.locator: Journal of Neurophysiology 108(2), published pp.578-579, Abstract and Introduction: task-level learning is operationalized as a training-related change in the empirical relation between movement speed and success, rather than movement along an unchanged relation

Journal of Neurophysiology 108(2), published pp.580-582, Methods and Results/Figs.2-3: 50 right-handed adults; day-1/day-5 testing at five imposed movement-time ranges; days-2-4 restricted-range training; trained groups improve across trained and untrained test speeds while the untrained control does not

Journal of Neurophysiology 108(2), published pp.583-584, Results/Figs.4-5: fixed-speed pre/post tests separate training-related kinematic changes from speed effects; trajectory variability falls markedly and mean trajectory changes modestly

Journal of Neurophysiology 108(2), published pp.585-586, Results/Fig.6: critical-zone entries decrease and successful online corrections increase after training; authors explicitly state these measures do not establish feedforward/feedback cause-effect mechanisms

Journal of Neurophysiology 108(2), published pp.586-588, Results/Figs.7-8: integrated squared jerk decreases across test speeds while submovement number, duration, and amplitude show no significant testing-day effect

Journal of Neurophysiology 108(2), published pp.588-589, Results/Fig.9 and Discussion: slow, medium, and fast restricted-range training groups show similar positive pre/post changes across five test speeds, indicating broad generalization beyond the practiced range

Journal of Neurophysiology 108(2), published p.592, Conclusion: task-level improvement is captured by the global performance-relation shift; kinematic changes include mean trajectory, variability reduction, and improved correction-related measures with invariant isochronous submovements; cortical/model-free mechanism is presented as conjecture

conditions: visually guided curved wrist movements without an externally imposed perturbation
performance assessed at fixed imposed movement-time ranges before and after three consecutive days of restricted-range practice
training range varied across slow, medium, and fast practice groups, with an untrained test-retest control group
population: 50 right-handed task-naive adults aged 18-38 years, randomly assigned to three trained groups and one untrained control group
task: guide a cursor through a semicircular channel with the nondominant wrist while satisfying imposed movement-time requirements and avoiding the channel boundaries
temporal_scope: baseline testing on day 1, training on days 2-4, and post-training testing on day 5
pre/post testing spans five movement-time ranges, including speeds outside each trained range

nodes.description: movement-time range imposed during the pre/post test blocks
three days of rewarded practice restricted to one designated movement-time range
empirical function relating imposed movement time to probability of completing the trajectory within the channel
positive pre/post change in success across the sampled movement-time ranges, including ranges not experienced during practice

task-level improvement is inferred from a training-related shift of the joint speed-success relation relative to baseline rather than from moving to a different operating point on an unchanged relation
day-1 and day-5 testing at five imposed movement-time ranges used to estimate the joint performance relation and its change
trial-to-trial variance of the task-relevant radial trajectory at matched test speeds
average radial trajectory at each matched test speed
integrated squared jerk of the trajectory, with lower values corresponding to smoother execution
proportion of movements entering the source-defined critical zone early in the trajectory
proportion of critical-zone movements that subsequently remain inside the channel
movement segmentation indexed by jerk-defined submovement number, duration, and amplitude

relations.description: the fixed-speed pre/post sweep estimates the joint performance relation and the change in success across the sampled difficulty range
restricted-range practice is followed by a positive shift across both practiced and unpracticed test speeds, whereas test-retest without practice does not show appreciable improvement
a positive shift of the joint relation relative to baseline satisfies the source's operational task-level improvement criterion
trial-to-trial task-relevant trajectory variability is substantially lower after practice at matched test speeds
mean trajectory changes after practice, but these changes are smaller than the reduction in variability
trajectory irregularity decreases after practice across test speeds
practice reduces early critical-zone entries and increases successful recovery from such entries
the observed changes are consistent with improved planning and online correction, but the source explicitly states that the measurements do not establish cause-effect control mechanisms
jerk-defined submovement number, duration, and amplitude show no significant testing-day effect despite improvement in task-level performance and trajectory smoothness
submovement number and amplitude vary strongly with imposed movement time, while duration changes only negligibly across the tested range
